voyage.name: Grand Egyptian Museum
voyage.alt: المتحف المصري الكبير al-Matḥaf al-Miṣriyy al-Kabīr
voyage.address: El Remayah Square, Cairo-Alexandria Desert Road, Giza
voyage.content: The Grand Egyptian Museum is the primary replacement for the venerable Egyptian Museum in Midan Tahrir, with much bigger exhibition, storage and workplace areas. Not to be confused with the Egyptian Museum or the Museum of Egyptian Civilisation. The main galleries cover Egyptian history from prehistory to the Greco-Roman period. The highlight is the Tutenkhamun gallery. At least four hours are needed to see the whole

voyage.name: Egyptian Museum
voyage.price: Adult 550 LE, student: 275 LE; photography (personal use) free; video 300 LE
voyage.content: Much of its collections were moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum in 2022.

voyage.name: National Museum of Egyptian Civilization
voyage.content: A relatively small museum, with a main hall, a textile hall, and a Royal Mummies Hall. The main hall covers Egyptian culture including prehistory, the dynastic period, Greco-Roman period, Islamic period, the modern and contemporary era, as well as exhibits of Coptic art and traditional art. The highlight is the underground hall of mummies.

voyage.name: Ibn Tulun
voyage.content: Arguably the oldest mosque in Cairo, built between 868-884.

voyage.name: Al-Azhar Park
voyage.content: A landscaped garden overlooking the Citadel

voyage.name: Khan El Khalily
voyage.content: Cairo's souk area where visitors will find many merchants selling perfume, spices, gold, Egyptian handicrafts.

voyage.name: Abdeen Palace
voyage.content: About 1 km east of Midan El-Tahrir, it was the royal residence until the Egyptian monarchy was deposed in 1952.

voyage.name: Pharaonic Village
voyage.content: Welcome to Egyptland! Especially if you've kids in tow, this showground and retail park will give you an instant Egypt-in-miniature. In Giza about 20 minutes drive from Downtown.

voyage.name: Dahshur Pyramids
voyage.content: For a contrast to touristy Pyramids of Giza, head south to the oldest known pyramid, the Red Pyramid. The neglected Dahshur Pyramids are interesting and worth a visit, considering its history and the hassle-free atmosphere. Also, see the weird Bent Pyramid there and hike around the area to the Black Pyramid. The Red Pyramid has an entrance to the inside, which you can climb down.

voyage.name: The Culture Wheel
voyage.content: The largest independent cultural centre in Cairo, offers concerts almost every night.

voyage.name: The Garden Theater
voyage.content: In Al-Azhar Park offers a range of musical performances. The venue is also a great place for an evening stroll.

voyage.name: Cairo Opera House
voyage.content: It hosted the Cairo International Film Festival in 2012 and screened some international films with very cheap subsidized ticket prices.

voyage.name: Egyptian Centre for Culture & Art
voyage.content: Egyptian Traditional music.

voyage.name: The Townhouse Gallery of Contemporary Art
Cairo Jazz Club
voyage.content: Live entertainment from local and international musicians, a great food and beverage menu (happy hour from 7-9PM) and a relaxed atmosphere. 7 nights a week.

voyage.name: Housaper theater
voyage.content: Mostly erroneously known and spelled as Hosabeer. A small theater which hosts cultural plays and concerts for independent artists.

voyage.name: Bab al-Futuh
voyage.content: One of three remaining gates in the wall of the old city. Marks the northern entrance of al-Mu'izz Street.

voyage.name: Al-Hakim Mosque
voyage.content: One of the largest Fatimid mosques in Cairo. It was originally decreed in 990 by the famously eccentric caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ("Ruler by God's Command") who, among other things, prohibited eating grapes or playing chess. Increasingly paranoid towards the end of his reign, he disappeared without a trace at age 36. The mosque has been used as a prison, a warehouse and an elementary school before being restored (

voyage.name: Bayt al-Sihaymi
voyage.content: Possibly the best-preserved Ottoman merchant house (16-17th century) in Cairo. Little visited and a place of quiet beauty. It's a museum now.

voyage.name: Qalawun Complex
voyage.content: Built by Mamluk Sultan Al-Nasir c. 1304 in honor of his father Qalawun. The complex contains a mosque, a madrasah (Islamic school) and the mausoleum where Sultan Qalawun is buried. The mausoleum in particular is often described as the world's second most beautiful, second only to the Taj Mahal, which it slightly resembles.

voyage.name: Maimonides Synagogue
voyage.content: Historic synagogue, the current building dates back to the 19th century but there has been a synagogue at this site since the 10th century.

voyage.name: Haïm Capoussi Synagogue
voyage.content: A former Kabbalah Jewish synagogue, built in the 17th century.

voyage.name: Church of the Virgin Mary
voyage.content: One of the oldest Coptic churches in this part of Cairo, dating back to the 10th century.

voyage.name: Midan Hussein and Sayyidna al-Hussein Mosque
voyage.content: One of the most sacred Islamic sites in the country and the Middle East, the mosque hosts the shrine in which the head of Ibn al-Hussein, the grandson of Muhammed the Prophet, is alleged to have been buried. The present building dates to 1870 and replaces a much earlier 12th century mosque. The Midan (square) before the mosque forms one of the most convenient access points to the Khan el-Khalili.

voyage.name: Al-Azhar Mosque
voyage.content: Founded in 970, al-Azhar is one of Cairo's oldest mosques and the world's oldest operating university.

voyage.name: Al-Azhar Park
voyage.content: The Al-Azhar Park is overlooking Darb al-Ahmar and the Citadel. Built on a garbage dump, it's today a green lung of Cairo and a pleasant area to stroll around and enjoy magnificent views of the city. It hosts a restaurant in a modern castle-style building and several good cafes. The theater has musical events almost every evening.

voyage.name: Sultan Hassan Mosque
voyage.content: Finished in 1363, this mosque was raised by the Mamluk Sultan Hassan and lying below the citadel and next to the much more recent rifaii mosque, it's maybe the primary example of the Islamic Mamluk dynasty. One of the largest mosques in Egypt and the Arab world, it was used as a school for different Islamic (Sunni) schools of thought and also contains a mausoleum.

voyage.name: Al-Rifa'i Mosque
voyage.price: , students . Includes admission for Sultan Hassan Mosque
voyage.content: Built in 1911, this mosque holds the tombs of a great number of Egyptian aristocrat families and also the last Shah of Iran, who retreated to Cairo after being ousted from power in his country.

voyage.name: Ibn Tulun Mosque
voyage.content: Raised in 877 by the Abbasid governor, this mosque has a style reminiscent of the Samarra mosque in Iraq, quite different from other Egyptian mosques. Built on a six-acre site, the mosque was large enough to accommodate all of the city's males for Friday prayer. The mosque has an open interior, and the minaret, the oldest in Egypt, is climbable for a panorama.

voyage.name: Gayer-Anderson House Museum
voyage.content: The mansion of the British Egyptologist R.G. Gayer-Anderson has a large and fascinating number of rooms displaying artifacts from the traditional life of the Egyptian elites.

voyage.name: Mosque of Qaytbay
voyage.content: Built in 1475.

voyage.name: Amir Taz Palace
voyage.content: Palace dating back to 1352.

voyage.name: Mohammed Ali Mosque
voyage.content: Built inside the Citadel by the famous Egyptian regent Mohammed Ali between 1830 and 1848, and site of his tomb.

voyage.name: Al-Gawhara Palace Museum
voyage.content: The palace of Egyptian ruler Mohammad Ali, built in 1814. The architecture is a mixture of European and Ottoman influences. Closed for renovation as of 2026.

voyage.name: Carriage museum
voyage.content: An exhibition of royal horse carriages, mostly from the 19th century.

voyage.name: Egyptian National Military Museum
voyage.content: The official museum of the Egyptian military. Contains a separate display for each war fought by modern Egypt. Airplanes and vehicles can be seen outside the museum. The architecture and design of the building might be more impressive than the exhibits themselves.

voyage.name: Manshiet Nasser
voyage.content: This neighborhood is home to large numbers of Coptic Christians. It is Cairo's largest enclave of Zabbaleen (garbage people) - Orthodox Christians who collect garbage throughout Cairo, sort through the garbage in their enclave, and sell the recyclables to earn their living. Being non-Muslim, they historically fed the garbage to pigs they owned, however in 2009 all pigs were killed by the government due to fear of "sw

voyage.name: Saint Samaan The Tanner Monastery
voyage.content: This is one of several decorated Coptic Christian churches, built inside caves, that were enlarged by the Zabbaleen where the Zabbaleen (garbage people) live and work.

voyage.name: City of the Dead
voyage.content: A Islamic necropolis and cemetery made of regular houses and wall but without roofs, inside of which and between still people are living.

voyage.name: Sayeda Aisha Mosque
voyage.content: Contains the tomb of Aisha bint Ja'far al-Sadiq, an early female Islamic scholar.

voyage.name: Muqattam Hills
voyage.content: The Church of Saint Simeon the Tanner is located at the foot of the hills, which Pope Shenuda III has visited several times. On a cliff wall is a depiction of prayers of Saint Simeon the Tanner and Pope Abraham. Muqattam Hills also provides a spectacular view of Cairo.

voyage.name: Khan el-Khalili
voyage.content: Cairo's giant souq (market). The khan, built in 1382, was originally a hub for traveling traders in the Fatimid era. Today, it's the most visited tourist market in Egypt. Almost any kind of souvenir can be bought here, but also quality produce is still to be found. Venture out of the tourist market and you'll find bustling local trade. Among other things you'll find Islamic clothes, scarves, belly-dancing equipment,

voyage.name: Tent Market
voyage.content: If your dream is to bring a Bedouin tent back from the country, this is the place to go. Dating to the 17th century, this is Cairo's last remaining covered market, and these days the wares on offer range far beyond tents.

voyage.name: Al-Gahsh
voyage.content: This budget restaurant, its name meaning "the mule," is purported to serve the best foul in Cairo. Its location--opposite one of Cairo's most revered mosques, Seidna Zeinab, and its proximity to Ibn Tulun--makes it a necessary part of any visit to this part of the city.

voyage.name: Egyptian Pancake House
voyage.content: This place serves sweet Egyptian pancakes (fateer) and western-style pizzas for LE20-35.

voyage.name: Naguib Mahfouz Restaurant
voyage.content: This upscale restaurant caters to tourists, but offers decent food in an air-conditioned setting.

voyage.name: Kushari
voyage.content: There is a good kushari shop at the corner of Al Mansouria and Saleh al Gaafari.

voyage.name: Pizzeria
voyage.content: Another good address is a pizzeria on Al Mansouria, near Arabian nights hotel.

voyage.name: Fishawy
voyage.address: In the street just behind Midan Hussein, Khan al-Khalili
voyage.content: For many years this was the preferred place of Nobel winner Naguib Mafhouz to meet with his friends. It's a great place to stop for tea and shisha and watch the world bustling by. Few places are better for having an easy conversation with people from all continents, as well as with relaxing Egyptians that speak English well.

voyage.name: Hotel Hussein Restaurant
voyage.content: Stay away from the food at this top-floor restaurant, but sipping a cup of tea above great views of the Midan Hussein by night is an enjoyable way to pass the time.

voyage.name: Hotel El Hussein
voyage.content: A basic hotel in an interesting area. Prices from LE45 for single rooms with shared baths on each floor to LE75 for doubles with en suite bathroom. AC is extra, but the ceiling fans works well. Ask for a room with a balcony.

voyage.name: Arabian Nights Hotel
voyage.price: for a single room and shared bathroom with AC, no heater
voyage.address: 10 Al Aaded Street, El Gamaliya, Cairo
voyage.content: A good hotel. There is a good roof balcony and free Wi-Fi access.

voyage.name: Mosque of Amr ibn al-As
voyage.hours: Open daily to non-Muslims, with the exception of prayer time
voyage.content: The Mosque of Amr ibn al-As was built (in Fustat) in 642, as Cairo's first mosque, following the Arab conquest of Egypt. It has been rebuilt several times, and most of what you see now is from the 18th century or later.

voyage.name: National Museum of Egyptian Civilization
voyage.content: A relatively small museum, with a main hall, a textile hall, and a Royal Mummies Hall. The main hall covers Egyptian culture including prehistory, the dynastic period, Greco-Roman period, Islamic period, the modern and contemporary era, as well as exhibits of Coptic art and traditional art. The highlight is the underground hall of mummies.

voyage.name: Umm Kulthum Museum
voyage.content: Located in the Monastirli Palace built in 1851, this museum is dedicated to Umm Kulthum, the famous Egyptian singer, songwriter, and actress.

voyage.name: Foustat Traditional Crafts Center
voyage.content: Museum and art centre dedicated to preserving traditional Egyptian arts. The complex houses a museum as well as shops selling traditional pottery and more. Artisans are at work on site most days and it's often possible to visit them and learn about their specific craft.

voyage.name: Ruins of Fustat
voyage.content: Fustat was the first Egyptian capital under Muslim rule, until it was deliberately burnet in 1168 to prevent its wealth to fall into the invading Crusaders. Very little of the city remains but it's possible to wander around the ruins.

voyage.name: Fustat Park
voyage.content: A massive new park located between the ruins of Fustat and National Museum of Egyptian Civilization. Hosting many events it also offers vantage points with views of the Pyramids and Cairo Citadel.

voyage.name: Babylon Fortress
voyage.price: No admission except for the Coptic Museum
voyage.content: Established by the Roman emperor Trajan, at the entrance of the former canal to the Red Sea, it became a fulcrum of the Roman occupation. Not long after the fall of the Empire, some of the very first Coptic landmarks were built upon its foundations.

voyage.name: Coptic Museum
voyage.price: admission LE280, photo permit LE50. Cards only, no cash
voyage.content: Established in 1908 and restored in 2015 to a high standard, the museum houses Coptic art and artifacts from Late Antiquity, from the late Roman empire through to the Islamic era and beyond. The presentation is clear in English, French and Arabic with generally well thought-out lighting. The display of mainly stone architectural fragments on the ground floor shows the development of the early fusion between Christian

voyage.name: Hanging Church
voyage.alt: St. Maria Church, Arabic: Kineeset al-Muallaqa
voyage.content: This church was built in 690, upon two bastions of the Roman fortress. Its nave is suspended over a passageway. Its wooden roof is supposedly shaped like Noah's ark.

voyage.name: Church and Monastery of St. George
voyage.hours: Church: daily 9AM-5PM (the monastery is not open to the public)
voyage.content: The Church of St. George dates to the 10th century or earlier, but was re-built in the early 20th century after a fire in 1904. Although it's sited in the Coptic quarter and gives its name Mar Girgis to the neighbourhood, it's not a Coptic church, but Greek Orthodox, as a sign at the entrance testily points out. (The Greek lettering is the clue.) Indeed it's the seat of the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria:

voyage.name: Church of St. Sergius and St. Bacchus
voyage.content: One of the oldest churches in Cairo, named for two early Roman martyrs, the interior is remarkable and distinctive. The basilica nave is decorated by 12 columns - 11 white marble and one red granite - and a beautiful iconostasis. It's built over a cavern where, supposedly, the holy family of Mary and Joseph reared the infant Jesus after their flight from Herod into Egypt. The cavern is usually accessible but has some

voyage.name: Ben Ezra Synagogue
voyage.content: Egypt's oldest surviving synagogue, dating to the 9th century and housed in the shell of a 4th-century church; restored in the 12th century and continually through to the 20th century. Charming interior but it's most famed for the Geniza Documents, discovered in the basement in 1890. Religious teaching was that old documents may not be discarded or destroyed if they contain the name of God, but reverentially buried.

voyage.name: Church of St. Barbara
voyage.content: Basilica style, multiple restorations from 5th to 20th centuries, its main interest is the collection of icons and relics.

voyage.name: Church of the Holy Virgin
voyage.alt: كنيسة السيدة العذراء في بابليون الدرج
voyage.content: Coptic church built in the 11th century.

voyage.name: Nilometer
voyage.content: Dating back to 861, the Nilometer is a large stone obelisk, now inside a small building, that was used to measure the level of the Nile was measured and therefore the tax rates for the farmers fixed. The Nilometer became obsolete when the Aswan Dam was built. While this may not sound particular specular, the interior of the small building is surprisingly beautiful. It reminds of the endless staircase by graphic artis

voyage.name: S.S. Nile Peking
voyage.hours: Cruises at 8-10:30PM on Sun, Tue, Thu, and Fri; 3-5:30PM Fri; also open when not cruising for dining along the riverside.
voyage.content: It's said that this is the boat from Agatha Christie's famous novel "Death on the Nile". The boat features a dining room, where set menus are served, the Shanghai Pub, and a deck from which to watch the Nile.

voyage.name: Souq El Fustat
voyage.content: A perfect place to buy souvenirs, many traditional artisans sell their wares here.

voyage.name: Egyptian Museum
voyage.price: , students . Tickets for videography (personal use only) are available at LE300 per camera. Photography is free
voyage.content: The museum is in a pink neoclassical building on the northern edge of Midan Tahrir. It's the product of the Egyptian Antiquities Service, established by the Egyptian government in 1835, to try to curb the looting of antiquities sites and artefacts. It opened in 1858 with a collection assembled by Auguste Mariette Pasha, the French archaeologist employed by Isma'il Pasha. After residing in an annex of the Bulaq palace

voyage.name: Abdeen Palace Museum
voyage.content: Collections are showcased on the lower floors in the Silver Museum, the Arms Museum, the Royal Family Museum, and the Presidential Gifts Museum, and the Historical Documents Museum was added in 2006. The palace, designed in the 1800s by a French architect, is worth seeing including the fountain courtyard.

voyage.name: Karim Francis Gallery
voyage.content: An art gallery

voyage.name: Museum of Islamic Art
voyage.content: Established in 1858 under authority of Khedive Tawfiq, the museum showcases pieces from mosques, homes, and palaces in Islamic Cairo.

voyage.name: The Postal Museum
voyage.content: This museum holds a plethora of historical exhibits relating to all things postal, from the history of the post system dating back to the time of the Pyramids to extensive stamp collections.

voyage.name: Yacoubian Building
voyage.content: For readers of Alaa al Aswani's best-selling book The Yacoubian Building. You can see the Yacoubian Building on Talaat Harb St where it still stands and where the story was based, although in the book it is referred to by its old name of Soliman Pasha St.

voyage.name: Prince Said Halim's Palace
voyage.content: Now derelict, this once beautiful building is worth a look for its beautiful architecture, baroque and classical archways. Built in 1896 by designer Antonio Lasciac from imported Italian marbles and stone. This once beautiful palace and gardens are a reminder of the 'Glory days of Cairo'. The building was nationalized by President Nasser, and eventually transformed into Al Nassareya Boys School, which quickly destroy

voyage.name: Egyptian National Railways Museum
voyage.content: At the eastern end of Ramses Station, this museum houses an amazing collection of steam locomotives, including that used by Empress Eugenie during her opening of the Suez Canal in 1863.

voyage.name: Al Fath Mosque
voyage.content: Completed in the early 1990s, this beautiful mosque is worth taking a look at.

voyage.name: Sha'ar Hashamayim Synagogue
voyage.content: This large synagogue opened in 1899 and was built in a style evoking ancient Egyptian temples.

voyage.name: Cairo Puppet Theatre
voyage.content: A fantastic way to spend an afternoon with the kids. The Cairo Puppet Theatre puts on a variety of shows including myths, fairy tales and fun children's stories.

voyage.name: American Research Center Egyptology, art and culture illustrated lectures
voyage.content: Lectures are held every Wednesday evening at 6PM during the academic year, open to all visitors, admission free.

voyage.name: Madbouli
voyage.content: Mostly Arabic bookstore with a range of political literature and other books.

voyage.name: Omar Effendi
voyage.content: A large iconic Egyptian, 150-year-old department store. Sadly, filled with Chinese and poorly made Egyptian clothing even now since its privatization and takeover by the Gulf Kuwaiti Sultan Centre Company.

voyage.name: Sednaoui Department Store
voyage.content: This once family-owned department store was nationalized in 1961 and now has the neglected feeling of an East German department store. It has 3 floors and has a grand sweeping staircase, and a glass roofed atrium worth seeing for that alone, if you like old architectural building designs. Sells very cheap fabrics on the 2nd floor where you can buy shirts, blouses, and curtain material and have made up by one of Cairo

voyage.name: El Shawarby St
voyage.content: The best street to bargain hunt for clothes and other goods. Don't be afraid to haggle; watch how the locals do it.

voyage.name: Shorouk Bookshop
voyage.content: Located on Midan Talaat Harb, Shorouk has two floors with a good selection of Arabic- and English-language books.

voyage.name: Talaat Harb Mall
voyage.content: Most famous for its downstairs fast food restaurants. Many cheap clothes stores are also in the vicinity of the mall which is located just above Midan Talaat Harb.

voyage.name: Attaba Bookstalls
voyage.content: Over 100 new and second hand book stalls all displayed in little Arabesque kiosks. Every type of book and magazine available in many languages. Usually hassle free and sellers are content to let you browse in peace. Always bargain, and the price will come down the more you buy. Very old books and classics up to newly released novels and magazines. A great place to find treasures and find a few books for your trip. Vi

voyage.name: AUC Bookstore
voyage.content: Great bookstore just minutes away from Cairo Museum in the AUC Hill House campus. Excellent selection of new books and all the usual Egyptian authors' works can be found there amongst the latest releases.

voyage.name: Al Bostan Mall
voyage.hours: Early till late everyday, after 1PM Fridays
voyage.content: Large old mall mainly selling computers, second-hand PCs and laptops, and computer accessories with some clothing and footwear stores and a few airline offices. Toilets on each of the 4 floors.

voyage.name: Eatery بيتزا القدس
voyage.content: Local take-away with incredible good pizza and Egyptian dishes. Pizza is for LE25.

voyage.name: Karam El Sham
voyage.content: There are big crowds and queues outside but for good reason. The staff makes a real effort to speak English to help you order and receive vour food after waiting. Both the sharwama and the rice are tasty.

voyage.name: Akram Gad Restaurant
voyage.content: Fast food restaurant, done Egyptian style. Usually very busy packed with locals, but very good food at a very non-tourist price. Good fuul and falafel. Large restaurant on 26th July St, just off Talaat Harb St, in downtown Cairo. They also offer a large schawerma 'Doner kebab sandwich' .

voyage.name: Koshary Abou Tarek
voyage.price: Medium LE20, Large LE25, Special LE30, rice with milk LE5 (Jan 2018)
voyage.content: Koshary is a filling pasta, tomato sauce, dried onions, chickpeas, lenses dish, and this restaurant is quite famous beyond Cairo for it and its speedy waiters. Rice with mild seems to be quite famous in combination (after) koshary.

voyage.name: Al Tahreer Koshary Restaurant
voyage.content: Popular koshari chain, serves koshari in various sizes though the small (1.4 kg/3 lb) is a good size portion. You can add hot sauce or a lemon sauce. Eat-in or takeaway.

voyage.name: Koshari Achmat
voyage.price: Koshari LE10, small salad LE3, rice with milk LE5
voyage.content: Decent and inexpensive Koshari.

voyage.name: Hardees
voyage.content: On Midan Tahrir Sq. Delivery 19066. Free Wifi.

voyage.name: Fish & Chips
voyage.content: The place is nostalgic of good old times. It's cozy and a bit quirky. Nice decorations. The crunchy bread slices are unique. It's a woman-run business. The shrimp stuffed fillet is delicious.

voyage.name: Oldish ( Restaurant & Cafe )
voyage.content: Tasty Egyptian meals. Besides the Oriental breakfast, they also offer English breakfast. Cozy, romantic, stylish place.

voyage.name: Le Grillon Restaurant & Garden Cafe
voyage.content: This is a warm and charming old-school restaurant. Serving traditional plates like mixed grill, fatoush and tahine salad, etc. Serves alcohol (beer) and shisha. Mains are around US$10 and soups & salads are US$3. Old songs are played. Many foreigners. Doesn't accept Visa.

voyage.name: The Greek Club
voyage.content: Mostly frequented by liberal and leftist Egyptians rather than Greeks, this is one of the best restaurants in Downtown Cairo. The Greek food offered is limited and the menu often erratic, but the dishes they do have in supply are very good and cheap. Alcohol (including imported spirits) is served and it's possible to just have a drink. Some of the best Kofte in Cairo. Closes down completely during Ramadan.

voyage.name: La Chesa
voyage.content: Serving fondues, and other traditional Swiss dishes, pizza, salads and patisseries, this is one of the better continental restaurants in Downtown Cairo.

voyage.name: Estoril
voyage.content: An old-school restaurant, it's been around since 1962, serving Egyptian food.

voyage.name: Beano's
voyage.content: Modern coffee chain, serves salad, sandwiches, etc.

voyage.name: Cilantro
voyage.content: Modern coffee-chain that also serves sandwiches, salads, etc. Wi-Fi available, credit cards accepted.

voyage.name: Costa Coffee
voyage.content: Modern coffee chain that also serves desserts and some sandwiches

voyage.name: Namaste Indian Restaurant
voyage.content: Exotic Indian dining experience.

voyage.name: Bird Cage
voyage.address: Semiramis InterContinental Cairo, Corniche El Nil
voyage.content: Reportedly the best Thai food in Cairo.

voyage.name: Tawfiqiyya Souq
voyage.content: Lots of coffee shops and lots of atmosphere.

voyage.name: Champollion Palace cafes
voyage.content: The cafes in the shaded alleys to the east and rear of the wrongly named Champollion Palace provide a lovely shaded respite from the noise of the city.

voyage.name: Odeon
voyage.content: This roof-top open-air hotel bar is also a restaurant, but most visitors prefer just to drink or have shisha. Beer (Stella or Saqqara) is LE15. Very popular among backpackers and foreign students. Open during Ramadan. Nice place to sit and have a drink, but poor service.

voyage.name: Sherlock Holmes pub
voyage.content: Atmospheric British-style pub with warm cosy atmosphere. Local and imported alcohol, moderate prices.

voyage.name: El Horreya Cafe and Bar
voyage.content: While noisy and crowded, this classic baladi bar (the Cairene take on a dive bar) is one of very few left in the city centre.

voyage.name: Cecilia Hostel
voyage.content: Things are not particularly clean, but the staff is generally nice. Free wifi. Rooms with and without bathroom available. A nice terrace is a meeting point especially in the night.

voyage.name: Dahab Hostel
voyage.content: This low-key, basic hostel is popular with the "no frills" travelers who want a basic room redolent of a Dahab beach experience in the big city and not much else. The Dahab is basically a collection of rooms on a garden rooftop in the Downtown area.

voyage.name: Museum Plaza Hostel
voyage.content: Comfortable air-conditioned accommodation for long or short term stay for work or study. Free WiFi, and laundry and kitchen facilities, are provided. Many rooms have balconies with partial view of the Nile.

voyage.name: Australian Hostel
voyage.content: Nice clean rooms, Friendly staff and AlTahrir Kosheri is just around the corner. Centrally located but hard to find. Just past the KFC and Radioshack, on the third floor.

voyage.name: Berlin Hotel
voyage.content: Budget style hotel on the lower end of the scale. Lift broken, no bathroom in room. Central Cairo, WiFi is available free of charge

voyage.name: Egyptian Night Hotel
voyage.price: Dorm rooms . Private rooms starting from .
voyage.content: This is a cozy new hostel located directly across from the Egyptian Museum, with views of the Nile. The inside is colorful, with very friendly staff. Many of the rooms come with balconies. Free WiFi. They offer a good continental breakfast with drip coffee.

voyage.name: New Palace Hotel
voyage.address: 17, Soliman El Halaby st, From Emad El Din st
voyage.content: Friendly staff, breakfast included, internet and printer access, free WiFi, rooms with bathroom and AC. 24h/day rooftop restaurant with a peaceful atmosphere, billard table and satellite TV.

voyage.name: Traveler's House Hotel
voyage.price: dorm room is and rooms start at
voyage.content: A new hotel in Cairo. Situated in downtown near the Orabi Metro station. Nice clean rooms with high ceilings and large windows. A large common room with a balcony is perfect for hanging out at the end of the day. Free breakfast, wireless internet and hot drinks throughout the day.

voyage.name: Arabesque Hotel
voyage.price: Private bathroom/shared bathroom: single US$23/16.75, twin US$26/21, triple US$29/26. Breakfast included, eighth night is free
voyage.content: It's next to the Egyptian Museum and Nile, and a great place to start exploring the city. The rooms are comfortable and the staff are friendly though somewhat unprofessional. The common room offers fantastic floor to ceiling windows for wonderful views of the city. You may be able to haggle for better prices.

voyage.name: Hotel Osiris
voyage.content: Hotel Osiris is a small, 17-room hotel on the top floor of a building near Bab el-Louk Square, and is a five minute walk from Midan Tahrir. The hotel provides clean rooms, some with private bathrooms.

voyage.name: Paris Hostel
voyage.content: Walid and his staff are great.

voyage.name: The Nile Ritz-Carlton
voyage.content: It's on the western edge of Midan Tahrir, close to the Egyptian Museum. It was built on the site of the former barracks of the British garrison of Empire days. This branch of the Hilton chain was the first major international hotel to be built in Cairo after the war. Very convenient for transport connections, for the Egyptian Museum and for Downtown.

voyage.name: Semiramis InterContinental Hotel
voyage.content: Opened in 1987, the Semiramis is one of Cairo's premier hotels. Contains the Bird Cage Thai restaurant and Sabaya Lebanese restaurant.

voyage.name: Talisman Hotel de Charme
voyage.content: The outside of the hotel may not be impressive, but this 25-room hotel provides clean, nicely decorated rooms, private marble bathrooms, air conditioning, free internet, and breakfast. The staff is friendly and helpful, providing high-end service.

voyage.name: The Ramses Hilton
voyage.content: Housed in a large, modern, purpose-built tower, the Ramses Hilton has great views from its upper floors, but lacks any real character. Still, the standards are what you would expect from the Hilton chain - as are the prices! Contains a business center, fitness center, outdoor pool, various restaurants and bars.

voyage.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
voyage.content: The oldest, the largest in Egypt, and the last surviving representative of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It was built to a height of 146 m (479 ft), but is now slightly reduced to a still towering 137 m (449 ft). Over 2 million blocks of stone were used to construct it, all through manual labour. Entry to the interior is on the north side, facing your approach.

voyage.name: Queens' Pyramids and Nobles' Tombs
voyage.content: All over the complex, but especially around the Great Pyramid, are various of these pyramids and tombs. On its eastern flank, you'll find the burial pits for his "solar boats", to carry him into the afterlife. Along the west flank are noblemen's tombs, such as those of Senegemib. Several of these tombs are open to visit and usually free of tourist hordes. There's no extra charge though baksheesh may be appreciated. E

voyage.name: Pyramid of Khafre
voyage.content: Khafre was the son and successor of Khufu. His pyramid (at 136 m) is slightly smaller than the Great Pyramid, but it's set on higher ground so it looks larger. A few blocks of the original limestone cladding survive at its tip; once all the pyramids were fully encased in this way. Entry to the interior is on the north flank.

voyage.name: Pyramid of Menkaure
voyage.content: Menkaure was probably the son and successor of Khafre. His pyramid is the smallest here at 62 m high, originally 66.5 m. Entry to the interior is on the north flank. Along the south flank are his Queens' pyramids, and on the east flank is his funerary temple.

voyage.name: Great Sphinx of Giza
voyage.content: Like pyramids, sphinxes (ancient and modern) are found in many lands; this one is specifically the Great Sphinx of Giza. It's a single block of sandstone 45 m long by 22 m wide, bearing a man's head upon a lion's haunches. It is understood, by mainstream archeologists, to have been carved out of the bedrock in the reign of Khafre, bears his likeness, and represents a guardian spirit of the necropolis. Its original na

voyage.name: Grand Egyptian Museum
voyage.alt: المتحف المصري الكبير al-Matḥaf al-Miṣriyy al-Kabīr
voyage.address: El Remayah Square, Cairo-Alexandria Desert Road, Giza
voyage.content: The Grand Egyptian Museum is the primary replacement for the venerable Egyptian Museum in Midan Tahrir, with much bigger exhibition, storage and workplace areas. Not to be confused with the Egyptian Museum or the Museum of Egyptian Civilisation. The main galleries cover Egyptian history from prehistory to the Greco-Roman period. The highlight is the Tutenkhamun gallery. At least four hours are needed to see the whole

voyage.name: Cairo Horse Riding School
voyage.content: This expat-run stable is situated inside a pristine Arabian horse ranch about ten minutes away from the Pyramids. The emphasis is on compassionate horsemanship and most of their school horses are rescues from the pyramid area which they have lovingly rehabilitated. They offer rides in the peaceful parts of the Giza desert and along countryside lanes, and longer rides to the Abu Sir Pyramid complex or jumping and dres

voyage.name: FB Stables
voyage.content: Popular with expats who keep their horses at livery, Karim at FB Stables is also great for a "tourist" type ride to view the Pyramids and Sphinx from the desert. Longer rides to Saqqara and Abu Sir can be arranged in advance, as can sunrise, sunset and moonlit rides. Other than the horses and good company, one of the best things about FB is their amazing rooftop terrace (with BBQ) with unrivalled views over the Pyram

voyage.name: Pyramids Sound and Light Show
voyage.hours: Daily 7PM in English, 8PM in another language
voyage.content: Distinctly kitsch but a fun evening if you're in the right mood. The "voice of the Sphinx" narrates (often inaccurately) the history of the Giza necropolis and its place in Egyptian history, while a laser display picks out details of the Pyramids and projects scenes onto the side of the Great Pyramid. There are two shows each evening, the first in English and the second in another European language: free headphone tr

voyage.name: Giza Zoo
voyage.content: The main zoo of Greater Cairo, founded in 1891. 2 km NE of Giza metro station but near the riverside, so if you're coming from downtown especially with children, it's easier to take a taxi. This is an old-fashioned zoo with a poor record for safety and animal welfare.

voyage.name: Orman Botanical Garden
voyage.price: LE5 per person and LE20 per car

voyage.name: Pharaonic Village
voyage.content: Advertised as "the living museum of Egyptian history, with replicas of an ancient village & the tomb of Tutankhamen." Actors dressed as ancient Egyptians play various scenes. Not very authentic, but can be interesting for kids. It has several museums and lots of souvenir shops.

voyage.name: Al Amir Perfume Palace
voyage.content: An overwhelming smell will hit you as soon as you walk inside, if you can stand the smell for more than a few minutes you can find some good deals on perfume.

voyage.name: Legends and Legacies
voyage.content: A relaxed indoor bazaar.

voyage.name: Beymen
voyage.content: Chic designer shopping including brands such Chanel, Prada, Gucci, and Christian Dior.

voyage.name: El Gizawy restaurant
voyage.content: At the pyramids entrance where the homestays are. Local specialties. The staff speaks sufficiently good English. Popular with the locals. Falafel for LE7, Egyptian pasta for LE25.

voyage.name: Nile Pharaoh Cruising restaurant
voyage.content: The boat features Pharonic decor, and offers a buffet with international and Egyptian cuisine, and belly dancing.

voyage.name: Khufu’s Restaurant
voyage.content: Restaurant with traditional Egyptian dishes and a view of the Pyramids.

voyage.name: Khan El Khalili
voyage.content: Has been open for over a century and is far and away the most stylish place for lunch or just a cold beer. Expect to pay Western prices.

voyage.name: El Mandara Coffee Shop
voyage.content: Local cafe with Hookahs and non-alcoholic drinks, black tea and Egyptian coffee, frequented by locals, inside and streetside sitting.

voyage.name: accommodations near the entrance to the pyramids
Marriott Mena House
voyage.content: Built in 1869 as a royal lodge for King Ismail the Magnificent, this magnificent palace has housed guests including Empress Eugenie and Prince Albert. Tastefully restored and located very close to the Pyramids. Rooms in the newer Garden wing from US$460. The Palace wing is closed for refurbishment as of 2026; be sure to ask for a room with a view of the Pyramids when it reopens. The main Pyramids gate is a 5-minute w

voyage.name: Hashemite Villa
voyage.content: Home of the late King Hussein of Jordan and his first wife Dina Abdel Aziz Ouan whilst they courted. They were married in Ma'adi Cairo April 15, 1955. The villa was abandoned for a long while, but has been repainted and refurbished and turned into office space for a petroleum company.

voyage.name: Wadi Degla Protected Area
voyage.price: LE 5 for foreigners, and an extra LE 5 to bring a car
voyage.content: A desert valley and canyon with limestone rock formations dating back 50 million years, that offers a great opportunity for taking a trek, jogging, rock climbing, and cycling. Wadi Degla is also a good spot for bird watching and viewing the various reptile species, plants, and deer that reside there. To get out of the park, either pay to have the taxi wait, or it's a 15-minute walk out to the main road where you can

voyage.name: M/S Nile Crystal Cruise
voyage.content: Two dining rooms, serving mainly Egyptian cuisine, with belly dancing, music and Tanoora dancers.

voyage.name: Café Greco
voyage.content: Place to get coffee and enjoy home-made waffles.

voyage.name: Fish Market
voyage.content: A pleasant fresh fish restaurant with a wide range of choice and good service. Choose your fish on ice before it is cooked. Fruit and alcoholic drinks available. Prices around EGP 120 per person including wine but strongly dependent on what fish you choose.

voyage.name: Fusion Restaurant
voyage.content: Situated along the Nile, Fusion serves Asian cuisine.

voyage.name: Gaya
voyage.content: Serves Chinese and Japanese cuisine.

voyage.name: Jared's Bagels
voyage.content: Numerous varieties of bagels, muffins, scones, Belgian waffles, and other options. Wi-fi available.

voyage.name: La Rosa
voyage.content: Serves pizza, pasta, and other Italian cuisine.

voyage.name: Lan Yuan
voyage.content: Chinese food ranging from dumplings, fried rice, and various rice, noodle, meat, and vegetable dishes, along with deep-fried bananas topped with ice cream for dessert. Eat in or delivery.

voyage.name: Lucille's
voyage.content: American diner named after owner Lucille Crooks. Improbably enough, according to Time magazine, they serve what may be the best burger in the entire world; perhaps a small exaggeration, but you'll certainly be hard put to find a better one in Egypt. Just don't expect any pork in your BBQ "bacon" burger. Also, a good place for American-style breakfast.

voyage.name: TGI Fridays
voyage.content: Outlet of the American restaurant chain located along the Nile in Ma'adi.

voyage.name: Fish Market
voyage.content: A pleasant fresh fish restaurant with a wide range of choice and good service. Choose your fish on ice before it is cooked. Fruit and alcoholic drinks available. Prices around LE 120 per person including wine but strongly dependent on what fish you choose.

voyage.name: Maadi Hotel
voyage.content: Once a four-star hotel, now distinctly worse for the wear.

voyage.name: Akhenaten Centre of the Arts
voyage.address: Eastern end of Sharia 26th of July

voyage.name: Cairo Tower
voyage.content: A distinctive landmark visible from most of downtown Cairo, the Cairo Tower was completed in 1961 and reaches a height of 187 m. Great day and night views over central Cairo and to the Pyramids from the revolving café and restaurant at the top. Be wary of security guards who will give 'tours' of the area and demand large tips, and note that the café requires a minimum expenditure of LE30. Although it's not written in

voyage.name: Gezira Centre of Arts
voyage.content: Displays an interesting collection of Islamic ceramics and galleries for temporary art exhibitions.

voyage.name: Khan al-Maghraby
voyage.content: Small, one-room gallery features young Egyptian artists

voyage.name: Museum of Islamic Ceramics
voyage.content: The museum is located in the former palace of Prince Amru Ibrahim in Zamalek.

voyage.name: Picasso Gallery
voyage.content: Contemporary Egyptian art gallery

voyage.name: Safar Khan Gallery
voyage.content: Contemporary Egyptian art gallery

voyage.name: Zamalek Art Gallery
voyage.content: Features modern Egyptian art.

voyage.name: Cairo Opera House
voyage.content: Egypt's most important cultural stage, home to much more than just the opera. Founded in 1869 as the Royal Opera House by Khedive Ismail, who commissioned Verdi's Aida, the original building was destroyed in a fire in 1971, so an entirely new one was built and opened in 1988. Today, it has two halls that can house 1300 and 500 people, as well as an outdoor theatre, and there are cultural performances virtually every

voyage.name: El-Sawy Cultural Wheel
voyage.content: An outdoor concert scene with modern Egyptian groups playing both Western and Middle Eastern music. The music might vary in quality, but it's a good place to meet young Egyptians. No alcohol.

voyage.name: Gezira Sporting Club
voyage.content: Includes four restaurants, swimming, lighted tennis, tennis pros and lessons, table tennis, squash, croquet, playing fields, walking tracks, exercise facilities, equestrian, basketball, children's play areas, saunas, bridge and board games.

voyage.name: Gezira Golf Club
voyage.content: A large public golf course. Admission for non-members is LE20, tournament fees are LE40.

voyage.name: Nile Maxim
voyage.content: Dinner cruise ship, operated by the Marriott, offers an à la carte menu, along with belly dancing, music, and other entertainment.

voyage.name: American University in Cairo Bookstore
voyage.content: Smaller version of the main campus bookstore downtown. Featuring AUC Press publications. among others.

voyage.name: Alef Bookstore
voyage.content: Provides a variety of book genres with personalized service in a cozy atmosphere for browsing and selecting books, plus reading area.

voyage.name: Diwan
voyage.content: Possibly Cairo's best English-language bookstore, also carries Egyptian and western music, videos and DVDs. A small cafe serves coffee and pastries.

voyage.name: Zamalek Bookstore
voyage.content: Small bookstore, with a large selection of English children's books and stationery products.

voyage.name: Concrete
voyage.content: Has high quality men's dress shirts that rivals anything in London, Paris, or Milan, and does free custom tailoring for trousers and suits. Ties are over priced, but otherwise, the prices are extremely reasonable given the quality.

voyage.name: Mobacco Cottons
voyage.content: Sells high-quality Egyptian cotton clothing, most of which is made in Egypt and exported. Prices are higher than other stores in Egypt, but the quality is comparable to stores in the US and Europe.

voyage.name: Sekem
voyage.content: Cairo's only organic food/health product store.

voyage.name: Sunny Market
voyage.content: Supermarket in the heart of Zamalek. Boasts a selection of familiar brands with a variety of local products.

voyage.name: La Trattoria
voyage.content: Excellent Italian food. Owned, and run, by the son of the famous actor Omar Sharif. Live music on Wednesdays.

voyage.name: Nile City
voyage.content: Stationary boat on the Nile includes several international franchises coupled an Egyptian grill and a seafood restaurant. Chilis, Johny Carinos, Fish Market & Studio Misr.

voyage.name: Didos Al Dente
voyage.content: This place serves pasta, and dishes are amazingly cheap, ranging from LE6-20. Small, intimate setting, making it an excellent spot for dates (despite its small setting, the waiters will let you linger/flirt at the table). Generally full from 5PM-close, waiting on the street outside is common, but it is worth the wait. They serve up some of the best pasta in all of Cairo. You pick your sauce, you pick the kind of past

voyage.name: Beano's
voyage.content: It has a West European style and serves food all day during Ramadan.

voyage.name: Deals Restobar Zamalek
voyage.content: Purportedly the best burgers in Cairo. Doubles as a pub. Open during Ramadan.

voyage.name: Euro-Deli
voyage.content: This place specialises in continental food and has several healthy salads and bagels in addition to very good coffee. Free Wi-Fi available and the place is popular with foreign students.

voyage.name: Maison Thomas
voyage.address: near Cilantro and Diwan on the north side of 26 July St.
voyage.content: Legendary establishment (Om Kolsoum once ate here) serving pastries, light food, and pizza. Owned by Coptic Christians. Beer available for take-away except during Ramadan.

voyage.name: Abou al-Sid
voyage.content: Owned by the conglomerate also responsible for Tabouleh (a rockin' awesome Lebanese restaurant in Garden City), and L'Aubergine, Abou al-Sid features high-end Egyptian cuisine and superb fresh juices. Very atmospheric. Make reservations in advance and dress up to get in.

voyage.name: L'Aubergine
voyage.content: 2nd floor turns nightclub at night. Closed during Ramadan.

voyage.name: Mojo's Lounge & Bar
voyage.content: Overlooking Nile. Shisha, wi-fi, parking, taxi service. Reservations required.

voyage.name: Sabai Sabai
voyage.content: Serves traditional Thai food in stylish settings and good service. This is a welcome addition to the Cairo Thai scene. Specify if you want the food spicy.

voyage.name: Le Pacha
voyage.price: About LE2500/person including drinks and service
voyage.content: A complex on a Nile boat with several restaurants and cafes inside the boat. Very tasty food and professional service for an upscale price. Le Tarbouche restaurant which serves hearty traditional Egyptian food. In particular, desserts are great. Also, allows to take home food. Has a good view of the Nile.

voyage.name: Drinkie's
voyage.content: A liquor store with a wide variety of spirits. One of the few places to find alcohol in this largely Islamic city.

voyage.name: Cilantro
voyage.content: Another branch in the Om Kolsoum Hotel on Abu el-Feda just north of the 26th July St Bridge crossing to Agouza. Part of a local coffee shop chain (think Starbucks) with pastries, light sandwiches, sodas, and free wi-fi.

voyage.name: Simonds
voyage.content: A small, long-established and highly popular café frequented by expats and students. Rather intimate, space is at a premium with just a few stools available or stand at the bar. Very good cappuccino. A great selection of sweets, pastries and juices is also on offer.

voyage.name: Sip
voyage.content: Specialty coffee with interesting cakes and good (comparing to Egyptian standards) coffee. Also good for working as WiFi is stable and inside area is comfortable.

voyage.name: Café Tabasco
voyage.content: Good coffee, a variety of Western and Arabic dishes including "American breakfast" and pancakes. Popular hangout for foreign students. Wireless internet available.

voyage.name: Costas Coffee
voyage.content: Another Cairo coffee chain, delicious coffee, small selection of pastries, sandwiches, and cold drinks. Best for take out coffee. Nile view

voyage.name: Euro Deli
voyage.content: Healthy food, homemade fries and salads. Good milkshakes. Wireless internet available.

voyage.name: Café de Paris
voyage.content: This place has drinks, sheesha and beer in nice garden surroundings with flat-TV running constant Arabic pop. Popular with nearby students from the AUC student quarters. Light food is also served.

voyage.name: Pub 28
voyage.content: Imitating a British pub frequented by expats and locals alike. International brands of liquor. Food served. Very popular, reserve a table if you are not content sitting in the bar (but you'll have to eat a meal then). Open during Ramdan. Stella , main dishes from .

voyage.name: Deals
voyage.content: Another popular pub haunt. Cable TV, DJ and house music. Pub menu. Open during Ramadan. Stella LE15, main dishes from LE25-60.

voyage.name: Harry's Pub
voyage.content: Karaoke-pub turns disco when the crowds are big enough. Local beer LE20.

voyage.name: Mayfair Hotel
voyage.content: An upper budget location - the people are nice, rooms clean, prices reasonable, and atmosphere peaceful. Free wi-fi, according to the website of the hotel.

voyage.name: Golden Tulip Flamenco Hotel
voyage.content: This hotel is more notable for its location than its service - rooms can be small, but comfortable. The service is good, and most room rates include breakfast - ask for a Nile view when booking. Free-of-charge wireless internet service is available.

voyage.name: Horus House Hotel
voyage.content: With equally friendly staff. Clean, serviceable rooms and a buffet breakfast.

voyage.name: Cairo Marriott
voyage.content: Housed in a former royal palace that was built to host Napoleon III and Empress Eugenie for the occasion of the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869. The old palace is still there, but the guest rooms (all 1069 of them) are housed in a modern tower block next to it. Still, the six-acre Omar Khayyam gardens are beautiful and it's a great place to have a drink or puff on a shisha. If you can afford the price tag, a stay a

voyage.name: Egyptian Museum
voyage.price: , students . Tickets for videography (personal use only) are available at LE300 per camera. Photography is free
voyage.content: The museum is in a pink neoclassical building on the northern edge of Midan Tahrir. It's the product of the Egyptian Antiquities Service, established by the Egyptian government in 1835, to try to curb the looting of antiquities sites and artefacts. It opened in 1858 with a collection assembled by Auguste Mariette Pasha, the French archaeologist employed by Isma'il Pasha. After residing in an annex of the Bulaq palace

voyage.name: Abdeen Palace Museum
voyage.content: Collections are showcased on the lower floors in the Silver Museum, the Arms Museum, the Royal Family Museum, and the Presidential Gifts Museum, and the Historical Documents Museum was added in 2006. The palace, designed in the 1800s by a French architect, is worth seeing including the fountain courtyard.

voyage.name: Karim Francis Gallery
voyage.content: An art gallery

voyage.name: Museum of Islamic Art
voyage.content: Established in 1858 under authority of Khedive Tawfiq, the museum showcases pieces from mosques, homes, and palaces in Islamic Cairo.

voyage.name: The Postal Museum
voyage.content: This museum holds a plethora of historical exhibits relating to all things postal, from the history of the post system dating back to the time of the Pyramids to extensive stamp collections.

voyage.name: Yacoubian Building
voyage.content: For readers of Alaa al Aswani's best-selling book The Yacoubian Building. You can see the Yacoubian Building on Talaat Harb St where it still stands and where the story was based, although in the book it is referred to by its old name of Soliman Pasha St.

voyage.name: Prince Said Halim's Palace
voyage.content: Now derelict, this once beautiful building is worth a look for its beautiful architecture, baroque and classical archways. Built in 1896 by designer Antonio Lasciac from imported Italian marbles and stone. This once beautiful palace and gardens are a reminder of the 'Glory days of Cairo'. The building was nationalized by President Nasser, and eventually transformed into Al Nassareya Boys School, which quickly destroy

voyage.name: Egyptian National Railways Museum
voyage.content: At the eastern end of Ramses Station, this museum houses an amazing collection of steam locomotives, including that used by Empress Eugenie during her opening of the Suez Canal in 1863.

voyage.name: Al Fath Mosque
voyage.content: Completed in the early 1990s, this beautiful mosque is worth taking a look at.

voyage.name: Sha'ar Hashamayim Synagogue
voyage.content: This large synagogue opened in 1899 and was built in a style evoking ancient Egyptian temples.

voyage.name: Cairo Puppet Theatre
voyage.content: A fantastic way to spend an afternoon with the kids. The Cairo Puppet Theatre puts on a variety of shows including myths, fairy tales and fun children's stories.

voyage.name: American Research Center Egyptology, art and culture illustrated lectures
voyage.content: Lectures are held every Wednesday evening at 6PM during the academic year, open to all visitors, admission free.

voyage.name: Madbouli
voyage.content: Mostly Arabic bookstore with a range of political literature and other books.

voyage.name: Omar Effendi
voyage.content: A large iconic Egyptian, 150-year-old department store. Sadly, filled with Chinese and poorly made Egyptian clothing even now since its privatization and takeover by the Gulf Kuwaiti Sultan Centre Company.

voyage.name: Sednaoui Department Store
voyage.content: This once family-owned department store was nationalized in 1961 and now has the neglected feeling of an East German department store. It has 3 floors and has a grand sweeping staircase, and a glass roofed atrium worth seeing for that alone, if you like old architectural building designs. Sells very cheap fabrics on the 2nd floor where you can buy shirts, blouses, and curtain material and have made up by one of Cairo

voyage.name: El Shawarby St
voyage.content: The best street to bargain hunt for clothes and other goods. Don't be afraid to haggle; watch how the locals do it.

voyage.name: Shorouk Bookshop
voyage.content: Located on Midan Talaat Harb, Shorouk has two floors with a good selection of Arabic- and English-language books.

voyage.name: Talaat Harb Mall
voyage.content: Most famous for its downstairs fast food restaurants. Many cheap clothes stores are also in the vicinity of the mall which is located just above Midan Talaat Harb.

voyage.name: Attaba Bookstalls
voyage.content: Over 100 new and second hand book stalls all displayed in little Arabesque kiosks. Every type of book and magazine available in many languages. Usually hassle free and sellers are content to let you browse in peace. Always bargain, and the price will come down the more you buy. Very old books and classics up to newly released novels and magazines. A great place to find treasures and find a few books for your trip. Vi

voyage.name: AUC Bookstore
voyage.content: Great bookstore just minutes away from Cairo Museum in the AUC Hill House campus. Excellent selection of new books and all the usual Egyptian authors' works can be found there amongst the latest releases.

voyage.name: Al Bostan Mall
voyage.hours: Early till late everyday, after 1PM Fridays
voyage.content: Large old mall mainly selling computers, second-hand PCs and laptops, and computer accessories with some clothing and footwear stores and a few airline offices. Toilets on each of the 4 floors.

voyage.name: Eatery بيتزا القدس
voyage.content: Local take-away with incredible good pizza and Egyptian dishes. Pizza is for LE25.

voyage.name: Karam El Sham
voyage.content: There are big crowds and queues outside but for good reason. The staff makes a real effort to speak English to help you order and receive vour food after waiting. Both the sharwama and the rice are tasty.

voyage.name: Akram Gad Restaurant
voyage.content: Fast food restaurant, done Egyptian style. Usually very busy packed with locals, but very good food at a very non-tourist price. Good fuul and falafel. Large restaurant on 26th July St, just off Talaat Harb St, in downtown Cairo. They also offer a large schawerma 'Doner kebab sandwich' .

voyage.name: Koshary Abou Tarek
voyage.price: Medium LE20, Large LE25, Special LE30, rice with milk LE5 (Jan 2018)
voyage.content: Koshary is a filling pasta, tomato sauce, dried onions, chickpeas, lenses dish, and this restaurant is quite famous beyond Cairo for it and its speedy waiters. Rice with mild seems to be quite famous in combination (after) koshary.

voyage.name: Al Tahreer Koshary Restaurant
voyage.content: Popular koshari chain, serves koshari in various sizes though the small (1.4 kg/3 lb) is a good size portion. You can add hot sauce or a lemon sauce. Eat-in or takeaway.

voyage.name: Koshari Achmat
voyage.price: Koshari LE10, small salad LE3, rice with milk LE5
voyage.content: Decent and inexpensive Koshari.

voyage.name: Hardees
voyage.content: On Midan Tahrir Sq. Delivery 19066. Free Wifi.

voyage.name: Fish & Chips
voyage.content: The place is nostalgic of good old times. It's cozy and a bit quirky. Nice decorations. The crunchy bread slices are unique. It's a woman-run business. The shrimp stuffed fillet is delicious.

voyage.name: Oldish ( Restaurant & Cafe )
voyage.content: Tasty Egyptian meals. Besides the Oriental breakfast, they also offer English breakfast. Cozy, romantic, stylish place.

voyage.name: Le Grillon Restaurant & Garden Cafe
voyage.content: This is a warm and charming old-school restaurant. Serving traditional plates like mixed grill, fatoush and tahine salad, etc. Serves alcohol (beer) and shisha. Mains are around US$10 and soups & salads are US$3. Old songs are played. Many foreigners. Doesn't accept Visa.

voyage.name: The Greek Club
voyage.content: Mostly frequented by liberal and leftist Egyptians rather than Greeks, this is one of the best restaurants in Downtown Cairo. The Greek food offered is limited and the menu often erratic, but the dishes they do have in supply are very good and cheap. Alcohol (including imported spirits) is served and it's possible to just have a drink. Some of the best Kofte in Cairo. Closes down completely during Ramadan.

voyage.name: La Chesa
voyage.content: Serving fondues, and other traditional Swiss dishes, pizza, salads and patisseries, this is one of the better continental restaurants in Downtown Cairo.

voyage.name: Estoril
voyage.content: An old-school restaurant, it's been around since 1962, serving Egyptian food.

voyage.name: Beano's
voyage.content: Modern coffee chain, serves salad, sandwiches, etc.

voyage.name: Cilantro
voyage.content: Modern coffee-chain that also serves sandwiches, salads, etc. Wi-Fi available, credit cards accepted.

voyage.name: Costa Coffee
voyage.content: Modern coffee chain that also serves desserts and some sandwiches

voyage.name: Namaste Indian Restaurant
voyage.content: Exotic Indian dining experience.

voyage.name: Bird Cage
voyage.address: Semiramis InterContinental Cairo, Corniche El Nil
voyage.content: Reportedly the best Thai food in Cairo.

voyage.name: Tawfiqiyya Souq
voyage.content: Lots of coffee shops and lots of atmosphere.

voyage.name: Champollion Palace cafes
voyage.content: The cafes in the shaded alleys to the east and rear of the wrongly named Champollion Palace provide a lovely shaded respite from the noise of the city.

voyage.name: Odeon
voyage.content: This roof-top open-air hotel bar is also a restaurant, but most visitors prefer just to drink or have shisha. Beer (Stella or Saqqara) is LE15. Very popular among backpackers and foreign students. Open during Ramadan. Nice place to sit and have a drink, but poor service.

voyage.name: Sherlock Holmes pub
voyage.content: Atmospheric British-style pub with warm cosy atmosphere. Local and imported alcohol, moderate prices.

voyage.name: El Horreya Cafe and Bar
voyage.content: While noisy and crowded, this classic baladi bar (the Cairene take on a dive bar) is one of very few left in the city centre.

voyage.name: Cecilia Hostel
voyage.content: Things are not particularly clean, but the staff is generally nice. Free wifi. Rooms with and without bathroom available. A nice terrace is a meeting point especially in the night.

voyage.name: Dahab Hostel
voyage.content: This low-key, basic hostel is popular with the "no frills" travelers who want a basic room redolent of a Dahab beach experience in the big city and not much else. The Dahab is basically a collection of rooms on a garden rooftop in the Downtown area.

voyage.name: Museum Plaza Hostel
voyage.content: Comfortable air-conditioned accommodation for long or short term stay for work or study. Free WiFi, and laundry and kitchen facilities, are provided. Many rooms have balconies with partial view of the Nile.

voyage.name: Australian Hostel
voyage.content: Nice clean rooms, Friendly staff and AlTahrir Kosheri is just around the corner. Centrally located but hard to find. Just past the KFC and Radioshack, on the third floor.

voyage.name: Berlin Hotel
voyage.content: Budget style hotel on the lower end of the scale. Lift broken, no bathroom in room. Central Cairo, WiFi is available free of charge

voyage.name: Egyptian Night Hotel
voyage.price: Dorm rooms . Private rooms starting from .
voyage.content: This is a cozy new hostel located directly across from the Egyptian Museum, with views of the Nile. The inside is colorful, with very friendly staff. Many of the rooms come with balconies. Free WiFi. They offer a good continental breakfast with drip coffee.

voyage.name: New Palace Hotel
voyage.address: 17, Soliman El Halaby st, From Emad El Din st
voyage.content: Friendly staff, breakfast included, internet and printer access, free WiFi, rooms with bathroom and AC. 24h/day rooftop restaurant with a peaceful atmosphere, billard table and satellite TV.

voyage.name: Traveler's House Hotel
voyage.price: dorm room is and rooms start at
voyage.content: A new hotel in Cairo. Situated in downtown near the Orabi Metro station. Nice clean rooms with high ceilings and large windows. A large common room with a balcony is perfect for hanging out at the end of the day. Free breakfast, wireless internet and hot drinks throughout the day.

voyage.name: Arabesque Hotel
voyage.price: Private bathroom/shared bathroom: single US$23/16.75, twin US$26/21, triple US$29/26. Breakfast included, eighth night is free
voyage.content: It's next to the Egyptian Museum and Nile, and a great place to start exploring the city. The rooms are comfortable and the staff are friendly though somewhat unprofessional. The common room offers fantastic floor to ceiling windows for wonderful views of the city. You may be able to haggle for better prices.

voyage.name: Hotel Osiris
voyage.content: Hotel Osiris is a small, 17-room hotel on the top floor of a building near Bab el-Louk Square, and is a five minute walk from Midan Tahrir. The hotel provides clean rooms, some with private bathrooms.

voyage.name: Paris Hostel
voyage.content: Walid and his staff are great.

voyage.name: The Nile Ritz-Carlton
voyage.content: It's on the western edge of Midan Tahrir, close to the Egyptian Museum. It was built on the site of the former barracks of the British garrison of Empire days. This branch of the Hilton chain was the first major international hotel to be built in Cairo after the war. Very convenient for transport connections, for the Egyptian Museum and for Downtown.

voyage.name: Semiramis InterContinental Hotel
voyage.content: Opened in 1987, the Semiramis is one of Cairo's premier hotels. Contains the Bird Cage Thai restaurant and Sabaya Lebanese restaurant.

voyage.name: Talisman Hotel de Charme
voyage.content: The outside of the hotel may not be impressive, but this 25-room hotel provides clean, nicely decorated rooms, private marble bathrooms, air conditioning, free internet, and breakfast. The staff is friendly and helpful, providing high-end service.

voyage.name: The Ramses Hilton
voyage.content: Housed in a large, modern, purpose-built tower, the Ramses Hilton has great views from its upper floors, but lacks any real character. Still, the standards are what you would expect from the Hilton chain - as are the prices! Contains a business center, fitness center, outdoor pool, various restaurants and bars.
